newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia looks to U.S. to keep military edge.
newsitem.headline: Australia looks to U.S. to keep military edge.

text.p: Australia, struggling to maintain its military superiority over neighbouring countries, will increasingly seek help from the United States to keep its hi-tech edge, Defence Minister Ian McLachlan said on Tuesday.

Australia has one of the most advanced armed forces in the southeast Asian region, but troubled government finances mean the defence budget has been barely maintained as Asian neighbours use their booming economies to spend big on defence.
"As a small, high-technology force, the ADF (Australian Defence Force) must be at the forefront of developments in technology and doctrine," McLachlan said in a speech.
The Australian military must maintain its strong scientific and technological base, he said.
"Apart from our own training and research, one area which is likely to grow will be cooperation with the United States' military forces," he said.
McLachlan foreshadowed an increase in the already growing military cooperation between the two traditional allies.

Australia's 16-month-old conservative Liberal-National government has adopted a more hawkish military stance than its Labor predecessors, strengthening military and strategic links with Washington, shielding defence from sweeping government spending cuts and redirecting money from administration to firepower and combat strength.
McLachlan has also pressed for a better ability to fight offshore, a shift from Labor's policy of protecting the country's vast coastline and air and sea approaches.

But Canberra is also boosting alliances with its Asian neighbours and McLachlan said on Tuesday all Australian officers must be "Asia-literate" -- with a knowledge of regional cultures and current affairs -- within a few years.
"After all, this region is the most important to our security," he said.
